rf-devices-001.question: In an AlGaN/GaN HEMT, a high-density two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) forms on the GaN side of the interface even though neither the AlGaN layer nor the GaN layer is intentionally doped. Which is the main reason?
choices: Electrons are supplied by a high concentration of residual donor impurities (oxygen or silicon) in the GaN layer and gather at the interface
The difference in spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization between AlGaN and GaN creates a positive charge at the interface, which electrons gather to compensate
Electrons are induced at the interface to form the 2DEG only when a positive voltage is applied to the gate, in the same way as the inversion layer of a MOSFET
rf-devices-001.explanation: Wurtzite nitrides such as GaN and AlGaN have a built-in polarization of the crystal itself (spontaneous polarization). When a thin AlGaN layer, with its smaller lattice constant, is grown on GaN, piezoelectric polarization from the tensile strain is added. The difference in polarization between the two creates a positive fixed charge at the AlGaN/GaN interface, and electrons gather in the triangular well on the GaN side to compensate it, forming a 2DEG of around 10¹³ cm⁻². The electrons come mainly from donor-like states at the AlGaN surface, not from impurities in the GaN. Because electrons are present even at zero gate voltage, an ordinary AlGaN/GaN HEMT is a normally-on device that is turned off with a negative gate voltage, which differs from a MOSFET that forms an inversion layer.

rf-devices-002.question: In a pHEMT (pseudomorphic HEMT) built on a GaAs substrate, why is a thin InGaAs layer used as the channel in which the electrons travel?
choices: Because InGaAs matches GaAs perfectly in lattice constant, so it can be grown at any thickness without regard to a critical thickness, free of defects and with high crystal quality
Because the bandgap of InGaAs is wider than that of GaAs, so the breakdown field of the channel rises and a high drain voltage can be applied to deliver high power
Because InGaAs has a narrower bandgap and higher mobility than GaAs and confines electrons in a deep well, and a thin layer absorbs the lattice mismatch as strain
rf-devices-002.explanation: InGaAs has a narrower bandgap and a smaller electron effective mass than GaAs, so the electron mobility and velocity are higher. The conduction-band offset to the surrounding AlGaAs is also larger, so the electrons can be confined in a deep quantum well. Donors are placed only on the AlGaAs side, away from the channel (modulation doping), so the electrons suffer little scattering from ionized impurities. The lattice constant of InGaAs is larger than that of GaAs and does not match, but if the layer is thinner than the critical thickness, the mismatch is absorbed elastically as strain and the layer grows without dislocations; this is what "pseudomorphic" means. The claim that the lattice constants match perfectly is wrong, and the claim of a wider bandgap is the reverse.

rf-devices-003.question: Which correctly defines fT and fmax, the measures of a transistor's high-frequency performance?
choices: fT is where the short-circuit current gain |h21| falls to 1 and fmax is where the maximum available power gain falls to 1; fmax can be higher or lower than fT
fT is where the power gain falls to 1 and fmax is where the current gain falls to 1, and fmax is always lower than fT regardless of the gate resistance
fT and fmax are both frequencies at which the current gain |h21| falls to 1, and they differ only in whether the load during measurement is 50 Ω or open
rf-devices-003.explanation: fT (the transition frequency) is the frequency at which the current gain |h21| with the output shorted falls to 1; for a FET, fT ≈ gm/(2π(Cgs + Cgd)), set almost entirely by the intrinsic gm and capacitances. fmax (the maximum oscillation frequency) is the frequency at which the maximum power gain obtainable with optimum input and output matching falls to 1; above it, the device can neither amplify nor oscillate. fmax depends on the gate resistance, the output conductance and the feedback capacitance Cgd, so for devices with the same fT, fmax can be higher or lower than fT depending on the structure. As a guide to the upper frequency limit of power amplifiers and oscillators, fmax has the more direct meaning. The explanation that swaps current gain and power gain, and the one that attributes the difference only to the load, are wrong.

rf-devices-004.question: For a HEMT, the current gain |h21| measured with the output shorted was 20 dB at 10 GHz. Extrapolating on the assumption that |h21| is inversely proportional to frequency and falls at −20 dB/decade, which is closest to fT?
choices: 1 THz
100 GHz
About 32 GHz
rf-devices-004.explanation: |h21| is a ratio of currents, so 20 dB is 10^(20/20) = 10 as a linear value. If |h21| is inversely proportional to frequency, |h21|·f is constant, and |h21| = 1 is reached at fT = 10 × 10 GHz = 100 GHz. 1 THz is the error of treating 20 dB as a power ratio, 10^(20/10) = 100. About 32 GHz is the error of taking the slope as −40 dB/decade, giving 10^(20/40) ≈ 3.16. In practice too, fT is found by measuring |h21| at a lower frequency and extrapolating the −20 dB/decade line to 0 dB. The unilateral power gain U falls with the same slope, so fmax is found by extrapolating in the same way.

rf-devices-005.question: The fmax of a FET is given approximately by fmax ≈ √(fT/(8πRgCgd)), where Rg is the gate resistance and Cgd is the gate-drain capacitance. Making the gate cross-section T-shaped (mushroom-shaped) cut Rg to 1/4 without changing the gate length, fT or Cgd. By roughly what factor does fmax change?
choices: 2 times
4 times
No change (fmax is set by fT alone)
rf-devices-005.explanation: fmax is inversely proportional to the square root of Rg, so cutting Rg to 1/4 makes fmax √4 = 2 times higher. 4 times overlooks the square root. The claim that fmax is set by fT alone is also wrong: parasitic elements such as the gate resistance, the feedback capacitance Cgd and the output conductance lower the power gain and govern fmax. Shortening the gate length raises fT, but the metal of a narrow gate has a large resistance. A T-shaped gate keeps the short gate length at the foot that touches the semiconductor while widening the top to increase the cross-sectional area and lower Rg. It is widely used in millimeter-wave HEMTs to achieve both a high fT and a high fmax.

rf-devices-006.question: Which is the main reason GaN HEMTs are widely used instead of GaAs FETs in high-power amplifiers for base stations and radar?
choices: Because the electron mobility of GaN is several times that of GaAs, so fT is much higher for the same gate length and high gain is obtained even at high frequencies
Because GaN has a narrower bandgap than GaAs, so a large current can flow at a low drain voltage, and the supply voltage can be lowered to raise efficiency
Because GaN's breakdown field is about 8 times that of GaAs, it runs at high drain voltages of 28–50 V, giving several times the output power per gate width of GaAs
rf-devices-006.explanation: The bandgap of GaN is about 3.4 eV, wider than the roughly 1.4 eV of GaAs, and its breakdown field is about 3.3 MV/cm, around 8 times the roughly 0.4 MV/cm of GaAs. It can therefore be used at high drain voltages of 28–50 V, and the high-density 2DEG produced by polarization carries a large current, so an output of several W or more per 1 mm of gate width is obtained, far above the roughly 1 W/mm of GaAs. The same output comes from a smaller device, so the capacitance is small, and operating at a high voltage raises the optimum load and eases matching. The availability of SiC substrates with high thermal conductivity also suits high power. On the other hand, the electron mobility is higher in GaAs, so the claim that GaN is several times higher is wrong. The claim of a narrow bandgap is the reverse.

rf-devices-007.question: A GaN HEMT is operated in Class A with drain voltage VDD = 28 V and knee voltage Vk = 4 V. The drain voltage swings sinusoidally about VDD with amplitude VDD − Vk, and the drain current swings sinusoidally about half the maximum current Imax = 1.0 A/mm (per 1 mm of gate width) with amplitude Imax/2. Which is closest to the output power per 1 mm of gate width?
choices: 12 W/mm
6 W/mm
7 W/mm
rf-devices-007.explanation: The voltage amplitude is 28 − 4 = 24 V and the current amplitude is 1.0/2 = 0.5 A/mm. The power of a sine wave is half the product of the amplitudes, so P = 24 × 0.5/2 = 6 W/mm. 12 W/mm is the error of taking the product of the amplitudes as the power and forgetting the factor of 1/2. 7 W/mm is the value with the knee voltage ignored and the amplitude taken as 28 V; once the drain voltage falls below the knee voltage the device can no longer carry the full current, so the swing cannot reach that far. The maximum drain voltage is 2VDD − Vk = 52 V, so a breakdown voltage that withstands it is also needed. For a GaAs FET at a drain voltage of around 8 V, the same reasoning gives only about 1 W/mm.

rf-devices-008.question: Which correctly describes current collapse in GaN HEMTs?
choices: A phenomenon in which, after a high drain voltage, electrons trapped at the surface or in the buffer layer raise the on-resistance and temporarily lower the maximum current
A phenomenon in which the channel temperature rises, the electron mobility falls and the current drops; it has nothing to do with traps and recovers as soon as the temperature falls
A failure in which the gate insulator breaks down under a high field and current no longer flows; once it occurs it does not recover until the device is replaced
rf-devices-008.explanation: When a high drain voltage is applied, a strong electric field forms at the drain-side edge of the gate, and electrons are captured by surface states or by traps in the buffer layer. The captured electrons act like a virtual gate and deplete the 2DEG beneath them, so the on-resistance rises and the current and output available under large-signal conditions fall. Electrons take time to escape from the traps, so pulsed measurements show a smaller current than DC measurements, and the effect causes lower output and efficiency and gain variation just after transmission. It is suppressed by passivation, which protects the surface with SiN or similar, and by field plates, which relax the field at the gate edge. The fall in mobility with temperature is a thermal effect and a different phenomenon. Nor is it a permanent failure.

rf-devices-009.question: In a SiGe HBT, what is the effect of increasing (grading) the Ge concentration in the base from the emitter side toward the collector side?
choices: Ge widens the bandgap, so grading it greatly raises the breakdown voltage between base and collector, allowing operation at high voltages
Ge lowers the hole mobility in the base, so grading it raises the base resistance but reduces thermal noise in return, improving the noise figure
Ge narrows the bandgap, so grading it creates a built-in field that accelerates electrons toward the collector, shortening the base transit time and raising fT
rf-devices-009.explanation: Adding Ge to Si narrows the bandgap. With more Ge toward the collector side, the conduction-band edge in the base slopes down toward the collector, creating a built-in field that accelerates the minority-carrier electrons. The transit time is shorter than when electrons cross the base by diffusion alone, and fT rises. At the emitter junction the bandgap difference reduces back-injection of holes, so the current gain is maintained even with a higher base doping, and the base can be made thin and low in resistance, raising fmax as well. Being made in the same process as Si CMOS (BiCMOS) is another major advantage, and its low 1/f noise makes it suitable for low-phase-noise oscillators and millimeter-wave circuits. The claim that Ge widens the bandgap is the reverse.

rf-devices-010.question: Which correctly describes the LDMOS (laterally diffused MOS) transistor?
choices: Because it uses a compound semiconductor such as GaAs, its fT reaches hundreds of GHz and it is the mainstream device for high-power millimeter-wave amplifiers and satellite transmitters
A lateral MOSFET on Si whose long drift region raises the breakdown voltage for 28–50 V operation; it is used mainly in high-power amplifiers for base stations below a few GHz
Its breakdown voltage is low, around 1 V, but in return it is easy to integrate on the same chip as digital circuits, so it is used in the transmit and receive circuits of handset transceivers
rf-devices-010.explanation: LDMOS is a lateral MOSFET built on Si, which obtains a high breakdown voltage from a lightly doped drift region between the channel and the drain, allowing operation at 28–50 V. The source can be grounded through the substrate to the back side, so the source inductance is small, which suits high-power devices. It can be made inexpensively in mature Si processes and is relatively tolerant of load mismatch, so it has been widely used in amplifiers for cellular base stations and TV broadcast transmitters. However, limits from the electron velocity and parasitic capacitances of Si restrict its usable frequency to about 3–4 GHz, and GaN HEMTs are used at higher frequencies and wider bandwidths. Calling it a compound semiconductor is wrong, and a low breakdown voltage suited to integration describes fine-geometry RF CMOS.

rf-devices-011.question: In fine-geometry RF CMOS, most of a transceiver, including the receiver, local oscillator and mixers, can be put on one chip, yet it is at a disadvantage for the final stage of a high-output transmitter. Which is the main reason?
choices: The finer the transistor, the lower its breakdown voltage (around 1 V), so the same power needs a large current and a low load impedance, increasing matching and wiring losses
Because even a fine CMOS device has an fT of only a few GHz, no gain can be obtained at all in the GHz range, so it cannot be used as the final transmit stage
Because third-order distortion arises only in CMOS amplifiers on Si and not in GaAs or GaN amplifiers, so leakage into adjacent channels increases
rf-devices-011.explanation: With scaling, the fT of CMOS has reached hundreds of GHz, and RF circuits can be integrated on the same chip as digital circuits, so most of a transceiver, including the receiver and local oscillator, can be put on one chip. On the other hand, the finer the transistor, the thinner its gate oxide, and the voltage that can be applied to the drain is limited to around 1 V. Output power is the square of the voltage amplitude divided by twice the load resistance (P = V²/(2R)), so delivering 1 W at a low voltage requires lowering the load to 1 Ω or less and passing a large current, which makes the losses in the matching network that transforms to 50 Ω and in the wiring large. Losses in the Si substrate also make inductor Q relatively low. An fT stopping at a few GHz describes old generations, and third-order distortion arises in amplifiers of every material.

rf-devices-012.question: A GaN HEMT amplifier takes DC power PDC = 40 W and input power Pin = 4 W and delivers output power Pout = 24 W. The thermal resistance from the channel to the bottom of the package is 3 K/W, and the bottom is at 85 °C. Which is closest to the channel temperature? (Assume all the output is at the fundamental and ignore heat dissipation through other paths.)
choices: About 205 °C
About 133 °C
About 145 °C
rf-devices-012.explanation: The power entering the device is the sum of the DC power and the input power, and what remains after subtracting the RF power leaving it becomes heat. Pdiss = PDC + Pin − Pout = 40 + 4 − 24 = 20 W, so the temperature rise is 20 × 3 = 60 K and the channel temperature is 85 + 60 = 145 °C. About 133 °C is the value with the input power forgotten, Pdiss = 16 W. About 205 °C is the error of assuming all 40 W of DC power becomes heat, without subtracting the power that leaves as output. The channel temperature is one of the most important quantities determining lifetime, and the thermal resistance is set by the thermal conductivity of the chip's substrate, the die attach and the package structure. This is why GaN is built on SiC substrates with high thermal conductivity.

rf-devices-013.question: Suppose the mean time to failure (MTTF) for a failure mechanism follows the Arrhenius equation MTTF ∝ exp(Ea/(kT)) with activation energy Ea = 1.5 eV. When the channel temperature rises from 150 °C to 175 °C, by roughly what fraction does the MTTF fall? Take Boltzmann's constant as k = 8.62×10⁻⁵ eV/K and 0 °C = 273 K.
choices: About 1/10
About 1/1.06
About 1/5.7
rf-devices-013.explanation: The MTTF ratio is exp((Ea/k)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)). With T₁ = 423 K and T₂ = 448 K, 1/423 − 1/448 ≈ 1.32×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ and Ea/k = 1.5/(8.62×10⁻⁵) ≈ 1.74×10⁴ K, so the exponent is about 2.30 and the ratio is e^2.30 ≈ 9.9: the lifetime becomes about 1/10. About 1/1.06 is the error of taking the ratio of absolute temperatures, 448/423, directly as the lifetime ratio. About 1/5.7 applies the rule of thumb that "lifetime halves for every 10 °C" to get 2^2.5; that rule corresponds to an Ea of about 0.5–0.6 eV near room temperature and cannot be used here. Thermal design translates directly into lifetime.

rf-devices-014.question: Which correctly describes the change when the i layer of a PIN diode is made thicker (with the same area and material of the i layer)?
choices: The capacitance under reverse bias increases, so the leakage in the off state falls and the isolation improves
The reverse-bias capacitance falls and the power handling rises, but the resistance at the same forward current increases and switching slows
The forward resistance falls in inverse proportion to the i-layer thickness and switching becomes faster, but the breakdown voltage falls
rf-devices-014.explanation: A reverse-biased PIN diode can be regarded as a parallel-plate capacitor with the i layer as the dielectric, and its capacitance is inversely proportional to the i-layer thickness W. Making it thicker reduces the capacitance and the leakage in the off state and also raises the breakdown voltage, so larger power can be handled. Under forward bias, the charge Q = Iτ injected into the i layer (τ is the carrier lifetime) lowers the i-layer resistance, but that resistance is roughly W²/(µQ), proportional to the square of W, so at the same current the resistance becomes larger. A thick i layer also takes longer to sweep out the stored charge, so switching becomes slower. An increase in capacitance is the reverse of the parallel-plate relation, and a lower forward resistance with faster switching is the property of a thinner i layer.

rf-devices-015.question: The capacitance of an abrupt-junction varactor diode is given by C ∝ (V + φ)^(−1/2), where V is the reverse bias voltage and the barrier potential is φ = 1 V. In a VCO whose resonant-circuit capacitance is formed by this varactor alone, the reverse bias is varied from 1 V to 15 V. Which is closest to the ratio of the maximum to minimum oscillation frequency? (Ignore other capacitances.)
choices: About 2.8
About 2.0
About 1.7
rf-devices-015.explanation: The capacitance ratio is Cmax/Cmin = ((15 + 1)/(1 + 1))^(1/2) = 8^(1/2) ≈ 2.83. The resonant frequency f = 1/(2π√LC) is inversely proportional to the square root of the capacitance, so the frequency ratio is √2.83 = 8^(1/4) ≈ 1.68, about 1.7. About 2.8 is the error of taking the capacitance ratio directly as the frequency ratio. About 2.0 ignores the barrier potential, takes the capacitance ratio as √15 ≈ 3.87 and then its square root; it overestimates the capacitance at small reverse bias. In a real circuit, fixed and wiring capacitances are in parallel, so the tuning range is narrower still. Hyperabrupt varactors, with an engineered doping profile, have an exponent larger than 1/2 and can tune the frequency over a wider range.
